name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,153

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Litvak's film has anecdotes about a secret police force

indicators.note: 'about' here means surrounding, so the first word's letters go round the rest

blocks.note: ana is a collection of anecdotes or sayings about a person
taken as written
the Stasi was East Germany's secret police

explanation.surface: A film by Litvak is said to be full of stories about some secret police.
explanation.walkthrough: Ana, a collection of sayings about someone, is a word mostly met in crosswords. Anatole Litvak directed the 1956 film with Ingrid Bergman as the claimed Romanov survivor.
explanation.definitionFit: Anastasia is the title of the 1956 picture directed by Anatole Litvak.

clue.text: Permitted, unlike Osborne's evidence

blocks.note: first meaning: allowed in
second meaning: John Osborne's play is Inadmissible Evidence, so the opposite of that

explanation.walkthrough: John Osborne's 1964 play is called Inadmissible Evidence; being unlike it means dropping the negative prefix.
explanation.definitionFit: Admissible means allowable, especially of evidence a court will accept, the reverse of Osborne's title.

clue.text: A Roman sculpture primarily associated with a roaring lion

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so each word gives just its opening letter

blocks.note: the first letters of the three words

explanation.surface: An ancient Roman statue is chiefly linked with a lion in full roar.
explanation.walkthrough: MGM's films open with a roaring lion beneath the motto Ars Gratia Artis, 'art for art's sake'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word for art heads the motto ringed round MGM's roaring lion logo, so it goes with that lion.

clue.text: Woodcutter cut out very small chess piece

indicators.note: a word that is cut short loses its tail end, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: tiny means very small
any chess piece is a man

explanation.surface: A lumberjack carves a tiny chessman.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Wizard of Oz the Tin Woodman was a woodcutter before his body was replaced with tin.
explanation.definitionFit: Baum's tin character was once a woodcutter and still carries his axe on the road to Oz.

clue.text: In which the French is at the foot, but it's translated first!

definitions.text: In which the French is at the foot, but it's translated first!

blocks.clueFragment: In which the French is at the foot
blocks.note: surface reading: a foreign film whose French dialogue is rendered at the bottom of the screen; setter's reading: the French word les comes at the end of the answer
the dialogue is turned into English, and the answer starts with a Latin word meaning under

explanation.walkthrough: Les, French for the, sits at the foot of the answer, while its opening is Latin for below: a joke on top of the plain meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: On a foreign film the translated dialogue runs along the bottom of the picture as captions.

clue.text: Turning up in Gilbert Kane I lay hidden

definitions.text: Turning up in Gilbert Kane I lay hidden

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means reading from bottom to top, that is backwards
hidden says the letters are tucked away inside the words before it

blocks.note: the letters run across these words

explanation.surface: The creature speaks: having popped up inside Gilbert Kane, it lay concealed there.
explanation.walkthrough: Gilbert Kane is John Hurt's character in Ridley Scott's 1979 film, the crewman from whose chest the creature bursts; the whole clue is the creature speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: In the film the extraterrestrial gestates unseen inside the crewman Kane before bursting out of his chest.

clue.text: Bengali on vacation has returned to Indian address

indicators.note: a word on vacation is emptied of its insides, leaving only its two end letters
something returned goes back the way it came, so these letters are read right to left

blocks.note: the first and last letters of Bengali
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone from Bengal, back from holiday, has come home to an Indian address.
explanation.walkthrough: BI and HAS together are read backwards. Sahib was the respectful form of address for a man in colonial India.
explanation.definitionFit: Sahib is a respectful title used when speaking to a man in India, so it is a form of address.

clue.text: Heavenly escalator for David Niven and Marius Goring

definitions.text: Heavenly escalator for David Niven and Marius Goring

blocks.note: surface reading: a celestial moving staircase

blocks.clueFragment: for David Niven and Marius Goring
blocks.note: setter's reading: the American title of their 1946 film A Matter of Life and Death begins with this word

explanation.walkthrough: Powell and Pressburger's A Matter of Life and Death, starring Niven with Goring as the heavenly Conductor, was released in America as Stairway to Heaven; its famous set is a vast moving staircase.
explanation.definitionFit: The film's great moving staircase to the afterlife gave the picture its American title.

clue.text: One of Schultz's newlyweds, like Brown, one who wanders aimlessly

blocks.note: honey is a golden brown colour
to moon is to wander about listlessly

explanation.surface: A newly married character from a Schultz picture, like a Mr Brown, drifts about without purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: John Schultz directed the 2005 film The Honeymooners.
explanation.definitionFit: A couple on their post-wedding holiday are honeymooners, as in the title of Schultz's film.

clue.text: Stoker inflamed by 25 mostly

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped
something inflamed is stirred up and agitated, so the letters are shaken into a new order

blocks.note: the answer to 25 across

explanation.surface: A man feeding a furnace is set on fire by most of Rambo.
explanation.walkthrough: Stoker looks like a furnace worker, fitting the fire imagery; it is the Dracula author, Bram Stoker.
explanation.definitionFit: Bram is the first name of Bram Stoker, the Irish author of Dracula.

clue.text: Film actor who worked with Stone?

blocks.note: first meaning: James ..., the British screen actor
second meaning: a craftsman who builds and carves in stone

explanation.walkthrough: The capital S makes Stone look like a director such as Oliver Stone; the question mark admits it is just the material.
explanation.definitionFit: James Mason was a leading film star, and a mason is a builder who dresses and lays stone.

clue.text: Anderson's hospital in Roman outpost

blocks.note: first meaning: Lindsay Anderson's 1982 satirical film ... Hospital
second meaning: the Latin name of the Roman province covering most of Great Britain

explanation.surface: A hospital run by someone called Anderson stands on a distant frontier of the Roman empire.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition gives only the first word of a film title, a licence this literary puzzle takes often.
explanation.definitionFit: Britannia Hospital is Lindsay Anderson's film, and Britannia was the Roman province on the empire's northern edge.

clue.text: Sarah Brown's employer, active in confusing vanity with morals

indicators.note: confusing things jumbles them up, so the letters that follow are mixed into a new order

blocks.note: a is the grammar abbreviation for active
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Sarah Brown's boss is busy muddling vanity up with morality.
explanation.walkthrough: Sarah Brown is the mission sergeant in the musical Guys and Dolls, whose Save-a-Soul Mission is modelled on this Christian charity.
explanation.definitionFit: In Guys and Dolls Sarah Brown works for a street mission of this evangelical charity, so it is her employer.

clue.text: Gaunt, we hear, a peculiar strain of Englishman

indicators.note: 'we hear' says the word before it is to be taken by its sound, not its spelling
peculiar means odd or out of the ordinary, so the next word's letters come out in an odd order

blocks.note: gaunt means thin and lean, lank
taken as written
the letters of strain, rearranged

explanation.surface: John of Gaunt, so we are told, was an unusual kind of Englishman.
explanation.walkthrough: Gaunt also suggests John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster, which is the clue's joke. Lancashire is a county in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: A Lancastrian is a native of Lancashire or Lancaster, so a particular type of Englishman.

clue.text: "… vindicating myself from the — of Will Maskery" (George Eliot)

definitions.text: "… vindicating myself from the — of Will Maskery" (George Eliot)

blocks.clueFragment: "… vindicating myself from the — of Will Maskery"
blocks.note: a quotation with a missing word: something one clears oneself of
the source: Mr Irwine's words in Adam Bede, where the plural noun for slanders fills the gap

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: the gap wants a plural noun for damaging remarks, from George Eliot's Adam Bede.
explanation.definitionFit: One vindicates oneself from slurs or slanders, which is what the missing plural noun means.

clue.text: One of which du Maurier associated with Kingston?

definitions.text: One of which du Maurier associated with Kingston?

blocks.clueFragment: One of which du Maurier associated
blocks.note: surface reading: some object or person that the novelist linked to a place
setter's reading: Kingston is the capital of Jamaica, so the thing in question is a Jamaica one, as in Daphne du Maurier's novel title

explanation.walkthrough: Kingston could be Kingston upon Thames; it is the capital of Jamaica, pointing to du Maurier's novel Jamaica Inn, and the clue asks for the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Jamaica Inn is du Maurier's novel; Kingston stands for Jamaica, so the answer is the kind of place her title names, in the plural.

clue.text: Koestler's fighters elated by drunken aristo

indicators.note: someone drunken staggers about, so the word after it is reeled into a new order

blocks.note: elated means happy, pleased
the letters of aristo, rearranged

explanation.surface: Arthur Koestler's combatants are cheered up by a tipsy nobleman.
explanation.walkthrough: Koestler's first novel, The Gladiators (1939), retells Spartacus's slave revolt.
explanation.definitionFit: Gladiators were the armed fighters of the Roman arena, and The Gladiators is Koestler's novel about Spartacus.

clue.text: "The subject is like a good sirloin which requires only to be basted with its own — " (Sir Walter Scott)

definitions.text: "The subject is like a good sirloin which requires only to be basted with its own — " (Sir Walter Scott)

blocks.clueFragment: "The subject is like a good sirloin which requires only to be basted with its own — "
blocks.note: a quotation with a missing word: what a roasting joint is basted with
the source, Scott comparing a subject that needs no embellishment to a joint cooked in its own fat

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: a good joint of beef is basted in the fat that runs from it as it roasts.
explanation.definitionFit: The fat and juices that run out of roasting meat are what a cook spoons back over it.

clue.text: When "If …" took place, depicting utter revolution at the end

indicators.note: a revolution turns something right round, so the word before it is read backwards

blocks.note: a term is an end or limit
to utter is to emit a sound

explanation.surface: When the film If.... was set, showing a complete uprising in its finale.
explanation.walkthrough: Lindsay Anderson's If.... (1968) is set in an English boarding school during the school session and ends with a pupils' armed uprising.
explanation.definitionFit: The film's action happens while the boarding school is in session, the period of the academic year when classes run.

clue.text: Editorial contribution's popular – it's expected in May

blocks.note: a leader is a newspaper's main editorial article; the 's adds S
hip means fashionable, in favour

explanation.surface: A newspaper's editorial piece is well liked, and something is anticipated next month.
explanation.walkthrough: May looks like the month; it is Theresa May, who became Conservative leader and Prime Minister in July 2016.
explanation.definitionFit: Theresa May was expected to give the country direction from the top, which is what leadership means.

clue.text: One capturing heart of Henry, England's leader

indicators.note: something capturing another holds it inside, so the first word goes round the second
'heart of' keeps only the middle letter of 'Henry'

blocks.note: ane is the Scots word for one
the middle letter of Henry

explanation.surface: A woman who won King Henry's heart and then led England.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Anne Boleyn winning Henry VIII; the definition is Queen Anne, who ruled England 1702-14.
explanation.definitionFit: Queen Anne was the English monarch from 1702, so she was the country's head of state.

clue.text: "Wand'rin' Star"? Yes, just like Ben Rumson goes!

definitions.text: "Wand'rin' Star"? Yes, just like Ben Rumson goes!

blocks.note: surface reading: the song title from the musical Paint Your Wagon, about a star that roams

blocks.clueFragment: Yes, just like Ben Rumson goes!
blocks.note: setter's reading: Ben Rumson, the drifting prospector who sings it, keeps wandering off the right path

explanation.walkthrough: Lee Marvin, as the prospector Ben Rumson, sings Wand'rin' Star in the film of Paint Your Wagon; a star that wanders has strayed from its course.
explanation.definitionFit: To go off the proper path is to wander from it, as the roaming Rumson does in the song.

clue.text: Camera techniques for filming prison docudramas?

blocks.note: the straight definition: ways of taking photographs with a long shutter opening
setter's reading: prison is doing time, and a documentary drama lays bare, or exposes, what happens there

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: serving a sentence is doing time, and a docudrama makes revelations about it.
explanation.definitionFit: Photographers use long, timed openings of the shutter, a technique named for the duration the film is uncovered.

clue.text: Leaving shortly, starts to live elsewhere – one like Richard Rowan

indicators.note: shortly means in brief form, so the word loses its final letter
the starts of words are their opening letters, so only those are taken

blocks.note: an exit is a leaving, a departure
the opening letters of live and elsewhere

explanation.surface: Departing soon, the first steps toward settling abroad, like a certain Richard Rowan.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Rowan is the writer returned from Rome in James Joyce's play Exiles.
explanation.definitionFit: Rowan is one of the title figures of Joyce's Exiles, a man who has lived banished from his homeland.

clue.text: One Andrew Rublev fabricated in Baltic Onyx

indicators.note: 'in' says the letters sit inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A work the medieval painter Andrei Rublev made out of Baltic onyx.
explanation.walkthrough: Andrei Rublev was the great medieval Russian painter of religious images.
explanation.definitionFit: Rublev painted holy images on wooden panels for Orthodox churches, the most famous being his Trinity.

clue.text: 12 involved with ICI, not Astra, could be a junior doctor

indicators.note: 'not' tells you to leave out the letters of the word that follows it
involved means tangled together, so the combined letters are mixed up

blocks.note: the answer to 12 down
taken as written
taken as written; these letters come out

explanation.surface: Someone from Lancashire tied up with chemical giant ICI rather than drugmaker Astra might be a young hospital doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove A,S,T,R,A from LANCASTRIAN to leave LNCIAN, add ICI and rearrange. ICI and Astra are both pharmaceutical companies, which suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A clinician is a doctor who treats patients directly, which a junior hospital doctor is one example of.

clue.text: Part of Hiram Bond played by Stallone

indicators.note: 'part of' says the letters are a stretch lying inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A role from the life of someone called Hiram Bond, acted by Sylvester Stallone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part' looks like a film role, which suits the definition, but here it signals the letters lying inside the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Sylvester Stallone played the Vietnam veteran John Rambo in First Blood and its sequels.

clue.text: Quickly, shortly

blocks.note: surface reading: fast; setter's reading: Mistress Quickly, the hostess in Shakespeare's Henry IV and The Merry Wives of Windsor
surface reading: soon; setter's reading: abbreviate her title

explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like adverbs of speed; Quickly is the Shakespearean hostess, and her title Mistress shortened is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The abbreviation for Mistress, Mistress Quickly's title, is the short form used before a married woman's surname.

clue.text: Variant of 19 originally childish

indicators.note: a variant is an altered version, so the word it governs has its letters rearranged
'originally' points to how a word begins, so only its opening letter is kept

blocks.note: the answer to 19 across
the first letter of childish

explanation.surface: A different version of a girl's name, first used in childhood.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: Nance is a pet form of Anne, the kind of name first used for a child.
explanation.definitionFit: Nance is a familiar diminutive of the name Anne, much as Nancy is, so it is a version of that name.

clue.text: Directions say it's cooked with lamb and bacon, for example

indicators.note: something cooked is changed from its raw state, so these words have their letters rearranged

blocks.note: compass points: east, south and south
the letters of say it's, rearranged

explanation.surface: A recipe's instructions say to cook it with lamb and with bacon.
explanation.walkthrough: Lamb and bacon look like meat but are Charles Lamb and Francis Bacon, both famous for their essays; the lower case is the disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Lamb and Francis Bacon are celebrated English writers of short prose pieces, so they are examples of the type.
